overview: Tasmanian Aboriginal history belongs to many local peoples, families and Countries across Lutruwita/Tasmania. Their communities developed knowledge suited to changing landscapes and seas, and continue today. This broad map label describes a cultural history, not a single kingdom, and its separated map intervals do not mark the beginning or disappearance of the people.

periods.title: Invasion and loss of Country
periods.summary: British colonisation began in 1803. Violence, land seizure and removal devastated Aboriginal communities. The Crown’s appropriation of the island displaced people whose own relationships with Country continued.

periods.title: Incarceration at Wybalenna
periods.summary: Wybalenna was established on Flinders Island in 1833. Exiled people endured coercion and severe losses while maintaining identity, ceremony and resistance to colonial control.

periods.title: Oyster Cove and continuing culture
periods.summary: Survivors were moved to Oyster Cove in 1847. Objects made during this period, including a kelp water carrier and shell necklaces, bear witness to continuing knowledge amid dispossession.

periods.title: Reclaiming putalina
periods.summary: The Aboriginal community reoccupied Oyster Cove as putalina in 1984. Community action made this place a focus of cultural continuity and the movement for land return.

periods.title: Land returned to the community
periods.summary: The Tasmanian Government formally returned putalina to the Aboriginal community in 1995. Its annual festival celebrates a living culture and community.

sections.title: Food, shelter and knowledge of Country

items.text: Patsy Cameron describes seasonal journeys between coastal and inland food places. Shellfish, crayfish, seabirds and eggs complemented wallaby, other animals and gathered plants. Safe travel by water required knowledge of currents, tides and weather as well as the skill to build a vessel.

Shelters varied with conditions: domed structures of branches, bark, mud and grass provided protection in cold, windy places, while arched windbreaks served some warmer coastal camps. Fire helped maintain pathways and encourage new vegetation. These practices depended on local knowledge rather than one uniform island-wide routine.

At Kutikina Cave, Ice Age deposits contained stone artifacts and large quantities of red-necked wallaby bones, including burnt and broken fragments. Layers of charcoal alternated with burnt red clay. Archaeologists interpreted these remains as evidence of repeated hunting, food preparation and fires inside the cave.

Moser’s study shows why archaeological illustrations need checking. A popular reconstruction included a hand stencil at Kutikina even though none had been found there. The picture combined excavated evidence with details known from other places and later records; the illustration itself cannot prove those details occurred at this cave.

A kelp water carrier sent to London’s Great Exhibition in 1851 survives in the British Museum. Its maker’s name was not recorded. The National Museum considers it likely to have come from the people confined at Oyster Cove, preserving both practical knowledge and a history of unequal collecting.

Dulcie Greeno’s necklaces combine lustrous maireener shells with smaller rice, button and other shells in carefully arranged strands. Collecting is seasonal work tied to coastal places. Women pass processing and stringing skills between generations while sharing stories and maintaining family relationships.

Older shellworking methods used animal-bone tools for piercing, natural fibres or sinew for stringing, and cleaning and polishing to expose the pearly surface. Later steel tools and finer threads enabled makers to incorporate smaller shells. These changes expanded an existing artistic practice.

sections.title: Watercraft and the renewal of skills

items.text: Early visitors described bark canoes travelling around southern Tasmania and offshore islands. Some carried a hearth at one end. Watercraft helped people reach bird eggs and seal hunting places, linking their construction with everyday food work.

Rex Greeno reconstructed paperbark canoes through reading, experiments with materials and his experience as a fisherman. He made the National Museum’s commissioned canoe with his son and grandson. The object records a deliberate renewal and transmission of skills, rather than uninterrupted survival of an ancient vessel.

In February 1846, men at Wybalenna petitioned Queen Victoria, asserting that they were free people and that promises made when they left their Country had not been kept. This written petition preserves their own political demands within a record often dominated by colonial officials.

The Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre’s palawa kani program has worked since the early 1990s to return language to spoken use. Researchers compare wordlists, manuscripts, recordings and remembered family knowledge, checking the reliability of people who originally wrote unfamiliar sounds down.

Palawa kani draws on evidence from several original Tasmanian languages; it is not an exact restoration of one of them. Community language workers analyse variant spellings and meanings, reconstruct sounds and develop teaching that allows children and adults to use the language together.

Community leadership has recovered some land and rebuilt institutions for caring for Country. The Aboriginal Land Council describes this work as a result of activism and continuing cultural responsibility, making land management part of contemporary history as well as remembrance.

ending.text: Colonial invasion brought catastrophic loss of life, dispossession and forced exile. It did not end Tasmanian Aboriginal people. Communities continue across Tasmania and beyond, carrying knowledge through family relationships, cultural practice and renewed institutions. The ending of an imported map interval must not be read as extinction.
